newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Traders say drop in Brazil soybean crop unlikely.
newsitem.headline: Traders say drop in Brazil soybean crop unlikely.

text.p: Rains were expected in most of Brazil's key soybean growing regions over the weekend and there was still time for parched areas to recover and produce a normal crop, traders said.
Parana was forecast to be cloudy and rainy over the weekend, according to Dora Azevedo at Brazil's National Institute of Meteorology (INMET).
In Rio Grande do Sul, a cold front was seen heading from the south of Uruguay into the extreme west of the state on the night of January 18, moving east and bringing scattered showers.
A second cold front was expected on January 20, moving across to reach Sao Paulo by January 21.
"We can talk of complete rain cover for the soybean growing regions," Azevedo said.

Traders said that although the weather in Rio Grande do Sul remained a concern, it was too early to predict crop losses in the state. They were still expecting Brazil to produce a record 1996/97 crop of 26.5 to 27 million tonnes.

"Until now the volume of rain in parts of Rio Grande do Sul is preoccupying but it's not enough to predict a drop in the harvest," said Carlos Murilo Pereira de Mello, director of commodities at Cotia Trading.
"The news always sounds more tragic than it really is," said one trader, referring to reports of dryness in the south.
"Many times we hear farmers have lost 10 percent here, 15 percent there, and by the time they harvest they've already lost 115 percent of the crop," concurred another.
There were scattered rains in the region between January 9 and 12 and more were expected at the weekend, he said.

"Some places received 100 mm and some have had no rain at all for 20 days," the trader said. "But most farms got some rain over the last 10 days. If they get rain now, they will still be good soybeans."

But concerns about the weather were slowing export trade as buyers worried their purchases may not be delivered and farmers were reluctant to sell in case a drop in the harvest drives up prices later.
Traders reported talk of a few sales of soymeal for mid-February to mid-March delivery, but could provide no further details on either the buyer or the quantity sold.
Low stocks were also hampering trade, some said.
"There has been demand from Asia for soyoil, including for prompt delivery, but we don't have enough stocks," according to one trader.

Internal soyoil prices were high in Rio Grande do Sul as many crushers took advantage of the post-Christmas, pre-Carnaval lull in activity to shut shop and carry out maintenance work ahead of the new harvest, said another.
"Buyers are saying they can get it cheaper in Argentina," he said. "There's no reason to sell for export if you can get higher prices on the internal market."
"Buyers are purchasing strictly what they need and not an ounce more," said another trader.

However, activity was expected to pick up soon as the harvest gets under way in Mato Grosso in around two weeks. Traders said advance sales for the region's crop were high, spurred by an expected drop in the U.S. 1996/97 soybean crop.
"I would say 70 percent of production in Mato Grosso has already been committed, all for April shipment," said a manager for a large trading firm, speaking from Campo Grande.
Independent consultants Safras e Mercado forecast Mato Grosso would produce just over five million tonnes in 1996/97.
